image.caption: Tobias Rausch has been elected as speaker in Saxony-Anhalt's parliamentImage: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: October 6, 2026
Far-right AfD candidate elected state parliamentary speaker

blocks.caption: Tobias Rausch has been in the Saxony-Anhalt parliament since 2016Image: dts-Agentur/picture alliance

blocks.text: Tobias Rausch, the far-right Alternative for Germany's (AFD's) nomination for speaker in Saxony-Anhalt's state parliament, has been elected with the help of the populist BSW party.
Rausch gained 48 votes from 82 eligible votes. There were five abstentions.

The AfD holds 39 seats in the parliament and the BSW five, giving Rausch the majority he needed to win the post, as the other parties combined — all of which reject working with the AfD — also hold 39 seats.
The result means that member of parties besides the AfD and BSW voted for him.

Rausch, 35, thus becomes the first member of the AfD — a party classified by domestic intelligence in Saxony-Anhalt as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" organization — to become speaker in a state parliament in Germany.
The new speaker is a real-estate entrepreneur by profession and has been a member of parliament for the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt since 2016.
The parliamentary session was accompanied by several anti-AfD protests in front of the parliament building.

articles.title: OpenAI admits response to Australian government hacks 'not good enough'
articles.summary: Top executive Jason Kwon tells hearing company has added "more precautions" to its training environments.

blocks.text: OpenAI has admitted its actions were "not good enough" after one of its rogue agents breached Australian government websites in June and said it had added more precautions to its training environments.

The company's chief strategy officer Jason Kwon faced a parliamentary hearing into AI on Tuesday in Sydney, saying the breach "should not have happened" and it "should have handled our response better". It took weeks before Australia was notified via an email to a generic inbox.
"We are sorry and we know we have work to do to rebuild trust with the Australian people," Kwon said.
Anthropic also appeared and said it had not found any cases of Australian breaches during a recent investigation.

An OpenAI agent went "rogue" and "infiltrated" a private statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare in June in what cyber-security experts said was the first hack of its kind.
Asked why OpenAI had not directly contacted government ministers immediately after it found out about the breaches, Kwon acknowledged it was a mistake.
"In retrospect, we should have done what you're suggesting," Kwon said, in response to a question by the committee on why it had not dialled the mobile numbers of government ministers.
"The reason why it happened the way that it did is I think people were thinking about this as a technical situation and they wanted to contact the technical counterparties but it's not good enough."
Kwon said the company has changed how it handles such incidents.
"Even if we don't fully understand the situation, we are just going to notify and start working through the situation collaboratively with the impacted party."

OpenAI has also added "more precautions" to its training environments since the incidents, Kwon told the 12-member committee which is made up of Labor, Liberal and independent MPs and senators who are looking at AI and its impact on Australia.
The company was also establishing a local taskforce in Australia to investigate "how to better manage the risks associated with increasingly capable AI".
Kwon told the committee that training models were now monitored in real time during tests, and an alarm was triggered if they interact with the internet in a way they were not meant to.
This meant that it had been able to alert the New South Wales government to another hack last week within 48 hours.
The company would also support a framework on mandatory disclosure of incidents, Kwon said, as it would set out "clear expectations".
"We were trying to come up with a standard to apply to our voluntary actions… based on our learned experience here, we should have been probably talking to more people about how to do that well."

Anthropic's head of safeguards Dave Orr said in the wake of OpenAI agents hacking tech platform Hugging Face in July, it had reviewed "hundreds of millions of transcripts" to detect any potential breaches of Australian government websites similar to OpenAI.
"We haven't found anything like this and we have looked," he told the committee.
The public hearings, which will continue until Friday, also heard evidence from arts and media organisations about copyright and their concerns on how AI models use their materials.

An opt-out model - where the onus would be on the artist to ask AI not to use their material for training purposes - was flawed and could means artists do not get paid for their content, the committee heard.
"In other words, Australia's artists will be the roadkill in the rush to this AI deal," said Annabelle Herd, chief executive of the Australian Recording Industry Association.

articles.title: Owner, businessman & player: Messi has big plans as a golden era ends
articles.summary: Lionel Messi's Argentina career will end in a friendly against Benin. BBC Sport looks at what next for the 39-year-old?

blocks.text: Lionel Messi is about to play his last match for Argentina.
On what will be his 208th appearance, the country's most-capped player and record goal scorer will bid an emotional farewell in a friendly against Benin at the Monumental in Buenos Aires.

Arguably Argentina's greatest ever player - only Diego Maradona comes close - announced his retirement from the national team on 31 August, six weeks after the World Cup final defeat by Spain, saying he had nothing more to give.
Coach Lionel Scaloni insists that if Messi ever wants to carry on, he can, and there is no embarrassment in changing one's mind. But that chapter seems closed.

His club career though goes on. The contract with Inter Miami runs to the end of the 2028 season, but it is reviewed year by year, and nobody close to him expects him to walk away a day before he has to.
In fact, it is quite likely he will renew it if he feels, mentally and physically, up for it.
Ask the people around him what comes after that and they smile, because Messi has never really planned beyond his next game.

Even so, the shape of what lies ahead is already in front of us. He will stay inside football, because he would struggle to live without it, but his other business interests stretch far outside the game.
Messi used to like the idea of being a sporting director or an adviser to the president, close to the decisions without all the travelling and the phone calls.
And asked recently whether he would rather be a coach or an owner, Messi chose owner.
A coach lives and dies by every Saturday and has to worry about far too many things for Messi's liking.

An owner shapes the direction of a club from a little further back. Having said that, he would be an owner who does not stop at approving the appointment of a manager and stepping away. He would want to be involved in everything.
The groundwork is being laid in Spain. UE Cornella, on the edge of Barcelona and in the fifth tier, is the nursery where young players grow. He bought it in April.
CD Eldense, in the second division, announced Messi as its new owner on 1 October, subject to authorisation from the Spanish sports council, the CSD.
Eldense will be the club that leads his football operation, but the target this season is not to get relegated, so former Villarreal boss Javi Calleja got the job with the arrival of the new owner.
The plan is to run both through people he trusts, who will act as a link between Messi and the clubs until the day he can give them his full attention.
For now he follows every Eldense match closely on his computer. After Eldense beat Real Oviedo by four goals to one, his first message as owner was an Instagram post that read "Aupa Deportivo".

The pull of his name has been felt as well. Around a dozen sponsors came forward within a couple of days, some of them brands that had been talking to the previous owners without ever closing a deal, and some that already have a relationship with him.
In Uruguay he and Luis Suarez founded Deportivo LSM in May 2025, and they won promotion to the country's third tier in its first season.

A network of more clubs was discussed at the start. But the sums needed to lift them up the divisions have cooled that idea quickly, and it is not on the table today. Messi's focus is to see whether Eldense can establish itself in La Liga.
There is a link to Miami as well. As part of his contract with Inter Miami, he will have some shares in the club when he retires. A franchise of his own is not part of the plan.
Could he go home to Newell's Old Boys, the club where he played as a child in Rosario? The idea has never been formally discussed.
It may have crossed his mind while drinking mate with Suarez, in the way a return to Barcelona or a spell at Napoli, the club of Maradona, might have.
Nobody close to the player expects it though. Everything is built around Europe and Miami, and the perfect home is waiting for the family in Castelldefels, close to the sea and Barcelona.
Newell's will still be close, because the club is one of the sixteen academies at this year's Messi Cup.
If owning clubs is one love, youth football is the other, and his regular presence at his son's games and the Messi Cup are the proof.
He puts his money and his time into a tournament for Under-16 academies, which began in 2025 with eight teams.
Last year, the organisers expected him to come to one or two games, perhaps only the final, but to everyone's surprise, he sat through every match on every day.
This year the teams doubled to 16, from 25 October at Inter Miami's facilities in Florida, including Atletico Madrid, Chelsea, Barcelona, Inter Milan, Arsenal, UE Cornella, and others.

Away from the pitch, Messi has built a portfolio that helps explain why Forbes put his net worth at about $1.1bn, external in June, with earnings of around $140m over the previous year split between football and business.
His best known endorsement is the lifetime Adidas deal he signed in 2017.
The most visible piece is MiM Hotels, six boutique properties from Ibiza to Andorra, which Melia has run under a rental agreement since 1 November 2025.
MiM takes its name from Messi and the Majestic hotel group, and runs the hotels inside its Melia Collection.
In Rosario, his family firm invests in Carrasco M, a development of 24 homes by the Parana river, with Ángel Di María's property agency handling the sales.
He is also a partner in the restaurant chain El Club de la Milanesa which plans to open five branches in Catalonia, the first in Castelldefels.
He has a mate collection with the drinkware giants Stanley, the brand's first multi-year deal with an athlete, and he gave his opinion on materials and colours.

The business side began with his father. Jorge Messi, who died in August aged 68, looked after his son's affairs from the start, and some of his early advice led the family into trouble with the tax authorities in Spain.
The company then grew into branches for TV production, marketing, media and commercial partnerships, among others, all well established by the time Jorge fell seriously ill.
Messi trusts the people who run them, some of them with him since his early days at Barcelona, and a thorough filter means he only gets offered and chooses what he is comfortable with.
He sets his own relationship with the business world, and nobody imposes anything on him.
In Miami last November, Messi told the America Business Forum: "Business is something that interests me. I would like to keep learning because I know nothing and I am just starting out."
The portfolio his circle has prepared is already impressive while he finds more football targets to keep the flame alive.

articles.title: India news: Opposition leaders march towards Election Commission
articles.summary: India's opposition is amping up pressure on Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to resign over alleged voter roll manipulation. DW has more.

image.caption: Congress party leader Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, center, and others hold placards during the opposition protest in New DelhiImage: Manish Swarup/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What you need to know
Here are our rolling updates from India on Tuesday, October 6:

items: Oppositon leaders are gearing up for a march to the Election Commission of India's headquarters to protest against poll body chief Gyanesh Kumar
Security has been heightened in key areas of central Delhi ahead of the demonstration
Voting has begun in by-polls in three Indian states and one Union Territory

blocks.text: Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
October 6, 2026
What is the controversy surrounding India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar?
Over the last week, mass protests against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar have been launched by India's opposition parties and also the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) youth-led movement.
The outcry comes after The Indian Express newspaper last month reported divisions ​in India's poll body over the revision of voter lists.
Kumar heads the three-member Election Commission which is overseeing the voter roll revisions.

The Indian Express reported that two of his fellow election commissioners raised at least 14 formal objections over 10 months regarding voter registrations, deletions and restorations, as well as control of electoral roll data, but those concerns were not taken into consideration.
Concerns emerged over the Election Commission's neutrality following the report.
Opposition leaders and critics say that those struck off the lists in the voter roll revisions include a huge number of minority voters.
They have accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi's BJP of using the exercise as a tool to secure future electoral gains, questioning the body's independence.

"The election commission is a puppet in the hands of the government. We are fighting to save ​our democracy," Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge, told the media ahead of the opposition march on Tuesday.

The Election Commission of India rejects allegations of wrongdoing and says the exercise removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and also prevents the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."
Kumar became the CEC in 2025 after being chosen by a selection panel led by Modi.
Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi, who was also a part of the panel, had opposed Kumar's appointment.

On Monday, India's top court issued notices to the Election Commission of India, the Modi government, Kumar and the other two election commissioners, seeking their response to a batch of petitions against the CEC over the alleged irregularities in the revision of electoral rolls.
If "there are decisions against the law ... We will take care of it," the Supreme Court said.

articles.title: Tigray rebel groups ‘forcibly recruiting boys as young as 15’ as fighting spreads
articles.summary:
Civilians try to flee as men and boys rounded up on streets by new alliance as Ethiopia conflict erupts again

As renewed fighting has threatened a fresh humanitarian crisis in the northern…

blocks.text: As renewed fighting has threatened a fresh humanitarian crisis in the northern region of Ethiopia, reports are emerging that a new alliance of armed groups in Tigray has been forcibly recruiting men and boys to its ranks.

Renewed conflict erupted on 23 September between Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which rules the region, shattering the fragile Pretoria peace agreement signed between the two sides in November 2022.
The latest fighting started after months of escalating tensions when the TPLF launched an attack in what it claims was a response to drone strikes by the federal government.
Witnesses who spoke to the Guardian described a broad campaign of forced recruitment in Tigray, targeting men and boys between the ages of 15 and 65.

The Eritrean Defence Forces and Amhara militias, which committed war crimes and crimes against humanity during the 2020-22 conflict, have switched allegiance and are now fighting in support of the TPLF.
Along with this new alliance, testimonies of forced recruitment, child soldiers and fresh humanitarian crises are emerging out of the already battered region.

Gezu*, 34, who fought with the Tigrayan forces in the 2020-22 war, lost many of his friends on the battlefield and was grateful to survive the deadly conflict. He was planning to start a family when he received a call from the TPLF authorities to join their armed group after the latest outbreak of hostilities.
“I refused to join the war,” he said. “I responded to them to kill me rather than ever force me back to the horrors of the battlefield.

“When they saw no one would join their army willingly, and people fleeing to the capital city, they started rounding up people from the streets. I didn’t want to leave my home town until things started getting worse.”

In the past few months, Tigrayans with the means to leave have been heading for the capital, Addis Ababa, fearing that war was coming. But on 23 September, Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to and from the Tigray region, stranding many people, after Tigrayan forces seized the airport in Mekelle, the capital of Tigray region.

Solomon*, a 52-year-old man who was able to flee to Addis Ababa, said: “The main targets are those between the ages of 15 and 40. I have seen the armed group of the TPLF rounding up people as young as 15 and 16 at gunpoint from the streets and public transportation areas.

“I know parents who tried to save their children by showing medical certificates. The officers don’t care whatever internal disease you have; they forcefully recruit anyone whose hands, eyes and feet work.”

Ephrem, 40, is a father of three who, fearing conscription, was planning to leave the region weeks before the fresh fighting erupted. “Every time I go outside the house, my wife and the kids are anxious. The kids cry fearing that I will be rounded up from the street.
“People who have money protect themselves and their children from the forced recruitment by bribing the officers. It is devastating; no one wants to join the war,” he said.

blocks.caption: Members of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front in the regional capital, Mekelle, last month after TPLF rebels seized the city’s airport. Ethiopian forces later retook it. Photograph: AFP/Getty

blocks.text: The Tigray region has been under siege for the past week, when citizens’ bank accounts were abruptly frozen by the federal government, leaving people unable to withdraw their money. The banks have since reopened with a daily withdrawal limit of 2,000 birr (£9) and with long queues forming outside.

Negus*, an elderly man in Mekelle, said: “We don’t know for how long the siege and the war are going to stay. A daily withdrawal limit of 2,000 birr can hardly afford to buy the skyrocketing food prices. It is impossible to leave this embattled region. There is no way for relatives outside to send medicine or cash. I am just hoping it all ends soon.”
Internet and phone communications were also cut off on the orders of the TPLF until this week, leaving families desperate for news of relatives in the region.
Meanwhile, the Ethiopian government has been accused of carrying out indiscriminate drone airstrikes and there have been reports of attacks by the opposition forces coming close to Addis Ababa.

An estimated 300,000 to 800,000 civilians died during the Tigray conflict, according to the British government. The Ethiopian army, Eritrean forces and Amhara nationalist “fano” militias, have previously committed grave atrocities against the Tigrayan population that amount to war crimes and crimes against humanity, according to the UN International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia. Tigrayan forces were also accused in an Amnesty report of committing atrocities during the war.
* Names have been changed to protect their identities

articles.title: Remulla flags Customs' alleged 'lack of data sharing' in smuggling cases
articles.summary: Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla has raised concerns about the Bureau of Customs' supposed lack of cooperation and data sharing, warning that missing or delayed documentation is hindering efforts to…

blocks.text: October 6, 2026 | 11:19am

Justice Secretary Jesus Crispin Remulla responds to senators’ questions regarding the Philippines’ residual obligations to the International Criminal Court (ICC) following its withdrawal from the tribunal, during a public hearing on Thursday, April 10, 2025.
Senate PRIB

MANILA, Philippines — Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla has raised concerns about the Bureau of Customs' (BOC) supposed lack of cooperation and data sharing, warning that missing or delayed documentation is hindering efforts to prosecute smuggling cases and strengthen anti-smuggling initiatives.

In a DZRH radio interview, Remulla said that while other government agencies have opened their records for joint anti-corruption and law enforcement efforts, the BOC remains hesitant to provide complete case documentation.
“Nagkaroon kami ng meeting ng Customs at saka ng DOJ (Department of Justice) para nga tumigil na ang kalokohang ito sa smuggling,” Remulla said.
(We had a meeting with Customs and the DOJ precisely to put an end to this nonsense in smuggling.)
“Ang problema nga kasi 'yung sa Customs, ayaw nila kumpletuhin ang documentation para ma-dismiss ang kaso,” he added.
(The problem with Customs is that they refuse to complete the documentation, causing the case to be dismissed.)
Remulla explained that while his office initiates cases or conducts investigations, their requests for necessary records are repeatedly met with inaction due to a lack of data sharing.

He noted that unlike the Bureau of Customs, the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) has already agreed to a data-sharing arrangement, adding that his office will now challenge Customs to do the same.
“Ifa-file namin ang kaso o kaya iimbestigahan namin sabay kapag hinihingi namin ang dokumento ayaw dumating ang dokumento. Walang data sharing,” Remulla said.
(We will file the case or conduct an investigation, but when we request the necessary documents, they refuse to provide them. There is no data sharing.)

Remulla voiced these concerns amid the government's heightened anti-smuggling drive, which has recently led to several contraband seizures by the BOC, as well as joint inter-agency operations with the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) and other law enforcement bodies.
The DOJ, the NBI and the BOC previously entered into a memorandum of agreement designed to curb economic sabotage. Remulla witnessed the signing.

articles.title: Sara Duterte trial recap, Oct. 5: Longest trial day as AMLC bares records
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court held its longest hearing yet on Monday, October 5, where the Anti-Money Laundering Council's chief testified to P4.4 billion in reported transactions involving Vice…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Senate impeachment court held its longest hearing yet on Monday, October 5, where the Anti-Money Laundering Council's chief testified to P4.4 billion in reported transactions involving Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband, including P319 million in remittances from China to his food company.

AMLC Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura testified as a prosecution witness under Article II of the impeachment complaint. That article accuses Duterte of amassing wealth "manifestly disproportionate to her lawful income," and of failing to fully and truthfully disclose her and her husband's assets in her statements of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALN) for 2022, 2023 and 2024.
His testimony took up the entire eight-hour session and drew repeated objections from the defense and sharp exchanges among senator-judges over whether the records should be disclosed at all.
The AMLC presentation had been moved from October 1 at the defense's request, after prosecutors also dropped former Sen. Antonio Trillanes IV from their witness list.
Monday's hearing came as House prosecutors have confirmed they would no longer present Article III, the bribery charge.
Here are the four highlights from the proceedings on Monday, October 5.
1. Court allows AMLC records, including dollar accounts, over objections

Before Buenaventura could testify, defense counsel Mark Vinluan moved to exclude him on the basis of the confidentiality provision in the Anti-Money Laundering Act, which bars the AMLC from revealing information in any manner.
The defense had attempted to convince the court that the AMLA provisions do not single out impeachment as an exception to its "absolute" prohibition for sharing AMLC records.
Presiding Officer Sen. Chiz Escudero denied the motion and sided with the prosecution in ruling that confidentiality provisions do not make AMLC reports "absolutely immune from compulsory process."
The impeachment court ruled that Section 8A "regulates the manner and conditions of disclosure" but "does not command absolute silence under every circumstance."

Escudero cited the Supreme Court's ruling in Republic v. Sandiganbayan and the Bank Secrecy Law's express exception for impeachment cases, which he said confirms "that bank secrecy is not an absolute bar to the constitutional accountability process."

He limited Buenaventura's testimony to the subpoenaed reports and said parts could be heard behind closed doors if needed. "This ruling does not authorize unrestricted public disclosure," Escudero said.

The ruling divided the senator-judges. Sen. Pia Cayetano noted that the anti-money laundering law, unlike the bank secrecy law, contains no exception for impeachment. She said reading one into it "puts a cloud over the impeachment proceedings." Sen. Imee Marcos similarly argued there was "no mention of an exception for impeachment proceedings."

Sen. Kiko Pangilinan, one of the law's two primary sponsors in 2001, said lawmakers intended the confidentiality rule to bind banks and not the AMLC. He said it "would be absurd that a private bank in an impeachment case trial can be compelled to divulge bank records" while the AMLC could not.

The dispute resurfaced in the afternoon, when Buenaventura, on direct examination, was made to testify on the figures of a foreign currency account. Marcos objected, saying it was "well established in both the Erap and Corona impeachments that foreign currency accounts are excluded."

Escudero overruled her with a prepared ruling that said the confidentiality provisions of the Foreign Currency Deposit Act must be read in tandem with the Anti-Money Laundering Act. Since banks are required to report covered and suspicious transactions to the AMLC regardless of currency, that means such information cannot be concealed by the council from the impeachment court.

The presiding officer also cited the 2012 impeachment trial of former Supreme Court Chief Justice Renato Corona, where then Ombudsman Conchita Carpio-Morales was allowed to testify on an AMLC report on the chief justice's foreign currency accounts.
2. What the AMLC records showed
Divinagracia said the records were meant to establish a baseline of Duterte's wealth and a "pattern of non-disclosure."
According to the AMLC summary, covered and suspicious transaction reports involving Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio, totaled P4.4 million from 2007 to 2025.

Buenaventura said about P1.63 billion of this was money coming into the accounts and P1.31 billion was money going out. The remaining P1.46 billion consisted of "fund transactions that could not be reliably classified as inflows or outflows due to insufficient, incomplete, or ambiguous sender and or beneficiary information," most of them from before 2014.

He said the total was lower than the roughly P6.7 billion the AMLC reported earlier because the court's subpoena covered a different period and all reporting institutions, not just banks, and because one bank, the Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI), corrected its reports.
Escudero had the AMLC chief confirm that the figures cover only covered and suspicious transactions and would not mirror the full bank records.

Buenaventura testified that seven inter-account transfers totalling P193.71 million, all in a single day on March 28, 2014, involved a BPI joint account of former President Rodrigo Duterte and the vice president.

He also identified a P20-million cash purchase of a life insurance policy on April 1, 2014, a debit of nearly P9.8 million from the same joint account in 2011, and a withdrawal of more than P9 million in 2013.
Buenaventura also confirmed that more recent records showed large cash movements in her or her husband's bank accounts during her term as vice president.

Six transactions all in a single day on Aug. 6, 2024, specifically two check encashments and four over-the-counter withdrawals of between P3 million and P15 million each, took P41 million out of her husband Manases Carpio's account in a single day.

Reports in the vice president's records showed a P2.37-million withdrawal at Landbank on Dec. 5, 2024. On Dec. 20, 2024, a P5.97-million withdrawal at BDO and a P1.7-million check encashment at Metrobank followed, 11 days before December 31, the cutoff date for assets declared in officials' SALNs.
Buenaventura also testified that Cale88 Foods Corp., the banana chips exporter company of Duterte's husband, received P319.33 million in remittances from mainland China and Hong Kong.
Broken down, the AMLC chief confirmed that of the 143 covered transaction reports on those remittances, 141 involved China and two involved Hong Kong.
The amount is close to the figure Trillanes presented at a press conference last week after withdrawing as a witness.
The records named Jinhua Dongxi Trading Co., Ltd. and China National Township among the counterparties.
Cale88 was among the companies Duterte declared she was a stockholder of in her SALN.
An AMLC information-sharing report also listed the vice president as the beneficiary of checks worth P14.88 million bought in 2011 and 2012 by Samuel Cang Uy and two others.
3. Suspicious transaction reports show Duterte's transactions were flagged by banks
The trial took a more surprising turn when the prosecution drew out Buenaventura's testimony on the suspicious transaction reports filed on the vice president.

Several of these reports on Duterte that were read in court were filed by banks and insurers on the basis of news reports, action that Buenaventura said is within the ambit of these institutions given the "threshold is suspicion" but which some senator-judges called unreliable.

Under the anti-money laundering law, banks and other institutions must file a covered transaction report for any cash transaction above P500,000 in a single banking day. A suspicious transaction report is filed when the institution sees red flags, regardless of the amount.
Buenaventura said the AMLC holds 34 suspicious transaction reports on Duterte from 2007 to 2025, while at least 30 such reports involved her husband, bringing the total to 55 for the couple.
The prosecutor had Buenaventura read some of the suspicious transaction reports.

For instance, two 2019 transactions by Duterte involving insurance premium payments to Mercantile Insurance Company Inc. were flagged for "graft and corrupt practices" after "several news outlets recently released a list of individuals and corporations identified as being involved in the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) flood control issue."
Buenaventura also read a suspicious transaction report filed by BDO Life Assurance on a Dec. 5, 2024 transaction, which cites "malversation of public funds and property."
Reading the narrative, the AMLC chief says: "The client is alleged to have misappropriated confidential funds to her office in the Office of the Vice President (OVP)."
Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano faulted the AMLC for passing on the reports and equated them to reading out "baseless rumors" in open court.

However, Sen. Kiko Pangilinan said he preferred to give banks the "benefit of the doubtm" while Sen. Risa Hontiveros said she would wait for testimony from the banks and the BIR before dismissing the banks' reports as rumors.

Pia Cayetano objected to the prosecution's on-screen summaries of the reports, saying they "do not show an accurate picture of what the witness is testifying to." She said: "This is like reading volume two of a comics and I never even saw volume one of the comic book."
4. Defense questions AMLC chief's authority; senator-judges push back

In cross-examination, Vinluan established that Buenaventura heads only the AMLC secretariat. He is not a member of the council itself, which consists of the Bangko Sentral governor, the insurance commissioner and the Securities and Exchange Commission chairman, and which must act unanimously.
Buenaventura confirmed he was appointed on April 14, 2026, eight days before he disclosed the couple's records to the House justice committee on April 22.

Asked whether the three council members gave him written authority for that disclosure and for his testimony on Monday, Buenaventura said he relied on information-sharing guidelines the council approved in 2022 and that he informed the council by memo. He said the House did not ask for such authority.

When Vinluan cited the administrative and criminal penalties under the anti-money laundering law, Divinagracia objected that he was bordering on badgering the witness. Sen. Raffy Tulfo then accused the defense of repeatedly trying to draw out redundant answers from Buenaventura and intimidating him.

Pangilinan said it was uncalled for to raise possible criminal liability over disclosures the court had already authorized. He also called out the defense for seemingly attempting to intimidate the impeachment court itself.
The defense will continue its cross-examination of Buenaventura on Tuesday, October 6.

articles.title: Youth groups ask SC to block law postponing barangay, SK polls to 2028
articles.summary: This is the second petition that was filed assailing the said law, which postponed the BSKE elections that were supposed to be scheduled on November 2.

blocks.text: October 6, 2026 | 11:03am
The logo of the Supreme Court at the Supreme Court Building in Manila.
Philstar.com / Ian Laqui
MANILA, Philippines — Youth groups challenged before the Supreme Court on Monday, October 5, the law that postponed the Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE).
This is the second petition filed assailing the said law, which postponed the BSKE elections that were supposed to be held on November 2.

The petitioners are seeking a Petition for Certiorari, Prohibition, and Mandamus, along with an extremely urgent prayer for a Temporary Restraining Order and/or Writ of Preliminary Mandatory Injunction to halt the law's implementation.

In their petition, the youth leaders strongly criticized the 20th Congress for repeatedly altering election schedules and terms. They pointed out that the legislature recently lengthened the term of barangay officials from three years to four years, and has now pushed it further to five years under the law.

“A very recent postponement of the Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE) through a ‘term-setting law’ was already ONE TOO MANY. ANOTHER, SUCCESSIVE resetting exposes the danger of allowing legislative form to prevail over constitutional limitations. It is a CIRCUMVENTION, IN BROAD DAYLIGHT, of the very five-point guidelines laid down by this Honorable Court in Macalintal,” the group’s petition read.
The respondents named in the petition are the Office of the President, Commission on Elections, House of Representatives, and the Senate of the Philippines.
The first petition was filed by election law expert Romulo Macalintal on September 28.
Macalintal argued that the law infringes on the electorate's right of suffrage under the guise of "fixing" the term of barangay officials at five years.
The last BSKE was held on Oct. 30, 2023, while the next elections were originally scheduled for December 2025.
Congress later moved the polls to November 2026 through Republic Act 12232, which also adjusted the term of office to four years.
Republic Act 12326, signed by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on September 24, meanwhile, postpones the elections by another two years to November 2028.

articles.title: Separatist party projected to win Quebec election, adding new test to Canada's unity
articles.summary: The Parti Québécois, which secured a minority, has vowed to hold an independence referendum in the years to come.

blocks.text: Canadian media projects the sovereigntist Parti Québécois (PQ) will secure a minority win in Monday's provincial election in Quebec, making Paul St-Pierre Plamondon the incoming premier.

It marks the first time the PQ has been in power since 2014. It could prove to be a test for Prime Minister Mark Carney, setting up confrontations with Quebec over issues like immigration and the monarchy.
The party has also pledged to hold a referendum on Quebec's independence, similar to an upcoming vote in province of Alberta later this month.
The majority French-speaking province has held other votes on this, in 1980 and 1995. Polls indicate only 30% of Quebecers back such a move.
Plamondon has said that vote would occur after US President Donald Trump is out of office.

Carney may find himself managing dual unity crises in different parts of the country, depending on the outcome of the separation vote in Alberta. Trump is due to leave office in roughly two years, meaning that if Plamondon keeps his pledge, a third plebiscite on independence would likely be scheduled for 2029 or 2030.
Separate from sovereignty, Plamondon has made it clear he is willing to fight Ottawa if it is seen as overstepping matters of provincial interest.
He suggested during the campaign that he was going to pressure Ottawa, external on issues like immigration, vowing to fight any increases mandated by the Carney government.
He also pledged to "abolish the monarchy in Quebec" and reroute money spent on its institutions to social services instead.
"We are going to do what we have to do to get the monarchy out of Quebec, repatriate those funds, and send them to social causes," he told reporters in late September.

For example, Plamondon suggested defunding Quebec's lieutenant-governor's office - responsible for representing King Charles III in the province - saying he would instead spend that money to tackle homelessness.
Plamondon was among the Quebec lawmakers who refused to pledge allegiance to the King in 2022, paving the way for a provincial law that now makes the oath of allegiance optional.
His plan to withdraw financial support for the lieutenant-governor's office is likely to face significant legal challenges, given the monarchy's central role in Canada's constitution.
Such a move would also put future Quebec laws in doubt, as one of the key roles of the lieutenant-governor is to give royal assent to new legislation.
Pressed about these hurdles, Plamondon has told reporters that he is ready for a legal battle with the federal government.
The success of the Parti Québécois on Monday is in part due to public fatigue with the previous Coalition Avenir Québec government.

Coalition Avenir Québec made safeguarding Quebec's identity and language central to its eight years in office, but its longtime leader, François Legault, eventually lost significant support among voters.
Efforts to revive the party by replacing Legault with a new leader, outgoing Premier Christine Fréchette, were unsuccessful.
Fréchette conceded her own re-election race in Trois-Rivières shortly before 22:00 local time. She said in a speech that she would work with St-Pierre Plamondon on the transition.
"Governing Quebec is the greatest honour I have ever had," she said. "I have Quebec tattooed on my heart."
The Quebec Liberal Party secured the second-most seats, while the Quebec Conservative Party gained seats.

Prime Minister Carney, who leads the federal Liberal party, remains popular in Quebec, though support for him had recently dipped, external as US President Donald Trump imposed new tariffs on Canada in August, following a breakdown in trade talks.
Quebec is among the hardest hit by the latest US tariffs, with experts at global forecasting firm Oxford Economics projecting a C$2bn blow for the province.
Carney congratulated Plamondon on his victory late on Monday and vowed to work together with the party.

"Building a stronger Québec is core to our mission of building a stronger Canada," he said in a post on social media. "I look forward to working with you to support Québec's businesses and workers impacted by tariffs, create more good jobs, work to end homelessness, and get more homes built across Québec."

articles.title: Samoa leader apologises for Nazi salute after video from 2007 emerges
articles.summary: Schmidt acknowledged that his actions "were inappropriate and capable of causing offence and hurt".

blocks.text: Samoa's prime minister has apologised after a video emerged of him giving a Nazi salute while saying "Heil Hitler" at a family gathering.

In the seven-second clip filmed in July 2007, Laaulialemalietoa Leuatea Schmidt is seen leading about a dozen people in the salute. "Raise your right hand, Heil Hitler!" he says, then thanks the group for responding.

Schmidt has acknowledged that his words and gesture "were inappropriate and capable of causing offence and hurt", adding that the clip was recorded at a private gathering and "not intended for the public".
"I reject Nazism, antisemitism, racism and all forms of political extremism," Schmidt said in a statement published on Facebook on Monday.
The footage was first reported by local outlet the Samoa Observer in a news story on Sunday.

It said the video was filmed at a Schmidt family reunion in July 2007, when Schmidt was deputy speaker of parliament and quoted a family member who said he was the master of ceremonies at the gathering.
Samoa, a tiny island nation of about 221,000 people, sits about halfway between New Zealand and Hawaii.
It was under Germany's control in the early 20th century, but the colonisation ended shortly after World War One broke out.
Schmidt, who has Samoan and German heritage, took office as the country's eighth prime minister in September 2025.
He wore a Jewish prayer shawl during his swearing-in ceremony and has made clear his support for Israel during the early days of his premiership, saying that Samoa "stood with Israel".
"If people around the world don't like it, that's up to them, but Samoa stands with the land of God... There is only one God our country believes in, the God of Israel," he had said.

articles.title: Trump says taxpayers will no longer fund ads touting administration
articles.summary: Trump faced criticism from across the political divide after at least $1.5 million in federal funds was spent on TV ads. He says his MAGA Inc. super PAC will pay for future ads.

image.caption: According to The New York Times, Trump ⁠personally directed the White House budget director to use taxpayer money for the TV spots [FILE: Sept 30, 2026]Image: Bonnie Cash/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture alliance

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump said Monday that taxpayer funds will no longer be used for television ads featuring him, which he claimed were a "standard thing to do," and said the cost will instead be borne by his super PAC.
The campaign-style ads, which cost at least $1.5 million (€1.34 million) in federal funds, drew criticism from lawmakers and ethics experts across the political divide.
What did Trump say about the ads?
Labeling the ads a "positive promotion for our Great USA," the US president said he decided to bear the costs himself and through his MAGA Inc. political action committee.

"This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
A White House official confirmed that MAGA Inc. would fund the ads going forward.
The MAGA Inc. super PAC had a war chest of more than $400 million by the end of July.
Trump ads warn of 'final battle'
The ads, which began airing in late September, feature Trump promoting his policies and warning against communism and of a "final battle" against "globalists."
They end with a disclaimer saying they were paid for by the US government.
Critics, including lawmakers from both parties, have questioned whether the ads violate restrictions on government propaganda and partisan political activity.
Democrats have said the administration transferred $20 million from the Department of Homeland Security to fund the ads and have called for independent investigations.
Trump has not said whether taxpayers will be reimbursed for the ads already aired.

articles.title: Fort Hood shooter to be executed by firing squad, in first since World War Two
articles.summary: The execution of Nidal Malik Hasan will be the first military execution since 1961 and the first by firing squad since the end of World War Two.

blocks.text: The Pentagon has announced it will execute a former US Army major by firing squad, the first such military execution in more than 60 years.
Nidal Malik Hasan, a US Army major and physician, fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, injuring another 32.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced on social media on Monday that Secretary of War Pete Hegseth had made the recommendation and President Donald Trump approved it.
It will be the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two.
Hasan was convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted murder by a jury panel of 13 officers, which unanimously recommended his death sentence.
Parnell said the Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution.
"Judgement day for Hasan has finally come," he wrote on X.
Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, killed 13 soldiers at the base in Texas in 2009 and later admitted in court he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes".
He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan.
The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base.
The attack took place in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.
Hasan is currently one of four inmates on the US military's death row.
A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law.
It also requires appellate review and a final judgment on its legality to move forward.

The US Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces deemed the military death penalty unconstitutional in 1983 but it was reinstated the following year by an executive order under then-President Ronald Reagan.
Military executions differ from those carried out at the state level.
The majority of executions in the US are carried out on the state level, with 27 states, the military and the federal government still having capital punishment as a legally available option.

Death by firing squad is rather uncommon. There was an execution by firing squad carried out last year in South Carolina, a first for the state and the first time the method was used in the US in 15 years.
Four other states allow the use of a firing squad, including Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma and Utah.
Trump has been a proponent of the federal death penalty and re-instated it through an executive order on the first day of his administration in January 2025.
Under his predecessor, former President Joe Biden, the justice department had issued a moratorium on the federal use of the death penalty.

The executive order signed by Trump describes capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".

articles.title: Bestselling author Steven Galloway's wife testifies on Day 1 of defamation trial
articles.summary: Former UBC professor and bestselling author Steven Galloway claims he was defamed by false accusations of sexual assault made by multiple people over a decade ago.

image.caption: Steven Galloway is pictured in 2014 at his former office at the University of British Columbia. The first day of court proceedings in a defamation lawsuit filed by Galloway, a bestselling author, began on Monday. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Former UBC professor and bestselling author Steven Galloway claims he was defamed by false accusations of sexual assault made by multiple people over a decade ago.
Former UBC writing professor claims he was defamed by false accusations of sexual assault

The wife of former University of British Columbia (UBC) professor Steven Galloway was the first witness to testify on day one of the defamation trial against four defendants he says falsely accused him of sexual assault.
Galloway’s accuser is a former student, "AB", who is the main defendant in the lawsuit. Others named as defendants are alleged to have spread the sexual assault claim, including on social media.
Katie Wagner told the court that Galloway was at a speaking engagement in Ohio in late 2015 when he first became aware of the accusation.
Wagner says that, when she arrived in Ohio to support him, Galloway was in a hospital on 72-hour suicide watch.

"He was in a hospital gown, he was upset, crying, shaking. He knew there was an accusation of sexual assault, but of course, he hadn’t sexually assaulted anyone — so there was a lot of us trying to figure out what was going on," she told the court.

items: Defendant apologizes to B.C. writer days before defamation trial to start

blocks.text: Galloway, a bestselling Canadian author, was never criminally charged — though he was fired from his job as a tenured professor and chair of the UBC creative writing department.
A report by retired B.C. Supreme Court judge Mary Ellen Boyd, commissioned by UBC, concluded the claims against Galloway were unsubstantiated.
After arbitration, he was awarded over $240,000 in damages from the university.
'Never going to be an end'
Wagner said Boyd’s report only served to sparked a "mob of people online" to repeat the accusations.
"There would be a flurry on Twitter — which was such a big thing," said Wagner. "I think there was a sense at that point … that there was never going to be an end to it."
Wagner testified that the accusations and resulting firestorm has been hard on their four children, finances, and life in general.

She said Galloway became extremely withdrawn, and at one point she found him trying to hang himself with a rope. She also recounted strictly controlling his medications for fear he would intentionally overdose.

items: Canadian authors criticize UBC's handling of Steven Galloway case

blocks.text: Galloway sued numerous people for defamation in 2018. His accusers fought the case all the way to the Supreme Court of Canada, claiming their accusations were protected speech.
The high court refused to hear the case, after a lower court said that if the defendants' arguments held, "there would be no legal consequences of any kind" to publicly calling someone a rapist.
At least nine of the defendants have settled out of court or issued apologies, including author Chelsea Rooney, whose lengthy statement of apology was published this past weekend.

Galloway is the author of novels including The Cellist of Sarajevo and The Confabulist. His lawyer said he is seeking special damages, to account for Galloway's former standing as a star in the literary world who had his career cut short.
AB has asked the court to keep her identity confidential over concerns an "online mob" would be unleashed against her.

Her counsel told the court that AB has attempted suicide. He said while news stories published about the case haven’t revealed her identity, people have named her in the comment sections under the articles.
The trial was originally scheduled for 60 days, but with fewer defendants, B.C. Supreme Court Justice Neena Sharma said it will likely take 20 days.
If you or someone you know is struggling, here’s where to look for help:

items: Canada’s Suicide Crisis Helpline: Call or text 988.
Provincial and territorial mental health support.
Kids Help Phone: 1-800-668-6868. Text 686868. Live chat counselling on the website.
This guide from the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health outlines how to talk about suicide with someone you're worried about.

articles.title: High-flying lawyer goes on trial for writing bad cheque allegedly to cover for collapsing firm
articles.summary: A Toronto lawyer who co-founded a law firm with his wife that collapsed in a spectacular flameout three years ago, when millions of dollars of client money was discovered missing from the firm's…

image.caption: Suspended lawyer Nicholas Julian Cartel, accused of fraud for writing a bad cheque to allegedly cover a shortfall in his law firm's trust account, leaves a downtown Toronto courthouse on Monday during a break in his criminal trial. (Aloysius Wong/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto·CBC Investigates

A Toronto lawyer who co-founded a law firm with his wife that collapsed in a spectacular flameout three years ago, when millions of dollars of client money was discovered missing from the firm's trust account, is on trial on a charge of fraud stemming from the police investigation into the case.
Nicholas Cartel is self-representing against criminal charge stemming from probe into $7M embezzlement

A Toronto lawyer who co-founded a law firm with his wife that collapsed spectacularly three years ago, after millions of dollars in client money was discovered missing from the firm's trust account, went on trial Monday on a fraud charge stemming from the police investigation into the case.

Nicholas Cartel, 62, faces one count of fraud over $5,000 based on allegations that he deliberately wrote a bad cheque for $300,000 in an attempt to cover up a shortfall in the trust account at Cartel & Bui LLP, the firm he ran with his wife.

The alleged fraud occurred in February 2023, when Cartel & Bui LLP was handling a property sale for a client. The law firm needed to pay out $2.22 million in proceeds to the client but didn't have sufficient funds in its trust account because Bui had been embezzling money from it for years, according to her own evidence in a separate civil case.
Bui is facing 32 criminal charges in a separate case stemming from the embezzlement.

The February 2023 incident foreshadowed a series of events in which more than 25 property owners and buyers in southern Ontario ran into problems closing on real estate deals because money was missing from the Cartel & Bui trust account.
One couple lost $2.16 million they had entrusted to the firm to buy a house in Toronto, while other clients — or home-purchase insurers — were out as much as $729,000.

Cartel is not facing criminal charges in relation to those other cases, and has long maintained his innocence. He says he operated a separate legal practice at the firm focused on class actions and litigation, while the theft of client money occurred in the real estate side of the business run by his wife, Singa Bui.
With respect to the criminal charge alleging that he deliberately wrote a bad cheque, Cartel does not deny writing it but says his actions didn't amount to fraud.

He also maintains that prosecutors have improperly withheld evidence from him and misleadingly presented other evidence. At the outset of his trial Monday, he told the court he intends to bring an application under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms to have his criminal charge stayed.
Bank employees testify

At the start of Monday's trial in provincial court in Toronto, prosecutor Dihim Emami called a witness from Royal Bank of Canada's investigations department to testify about records associated with the personal chequing account on which the $300,000 cheque was drawn.

The witness, Adkin Holder, a former Toronto police fraud-squad detective, testified that the account's opening documents showed it belonged to Cartel and that for months before the bad cheque was written, the account had a negative balance.

He said that because of that, a $300,000 cheque would have failed to cash, and the receiving bank could have been at risk of losing the money if it was unable to recover it from the person who wrote the cheque.
Cartel later asked Holder whether it was possible the account was in fact a joint account at the time the bad cheque was written, which Holder agreed was possible.
Prosecutors then entered records showing that the account statements bore only Cartel's name, while statements for other joint accounts bore both his name and Bui's.
A second witness, from TD Bank, where the law firm had its trust account, began testifying Monday afternoon about transactions in that account and is expected to resume Tuesday.
Already jailed for contempt of court

Cartel has already spent 30 days in jail over the collapse of his firm, after a judge in separate civil lawsuits against him and his wife ruled in August 2024 that he had committed contempt of court by failing to produce records or answer questions about where the missing trust-account money went.
He filed an appeal of that ruling, but it was dismissed this past August because he failed to move it forward.
He is also on the hook for millions of dollars in default judgments against him obtained by former clients of his firm, though has said he will contest them.
His attempt to overturn one of those judgments, for $500,000, was rejected by the Ontario Court of Appeal in February.
Defendant dismissed his criminal lawyer

Cartel hired veteran criminal lawyer Richard Posner to defend him late last year, but split with Posner 4½ months later amid a dispute over his fees and trial strategy, according to records obtained by CBC from a separate case in which Cartel challenged Posner's billings.

Those records show Cartel wanted his lawyer to try to get his charge dismissed as an abuse of process — a rare remedy available when a defendant can show that the prosecution's conduct seriously compromised the accused's right to a fair trial.
"In my respectful view, there is no basis for advancing an abuse of process claim in this case," Posner emailed Cartel, according to documents from their fee dispute.
"If you want to bring this motion, you will need to discharge me and find another lawyer or represent yourself."

items: Lawyer couple accused of stealing millions from homebuyers while law society stalled
Lawyers at centre of $7M real estate embezzlement case charged with fraud

blocks.text: At another point, Cartel and Posner differed over whether they should agree at trial to certain of the prosecution's alleged facts.
"Why dispute or make the Crown prove things that are plain and obvious from the business records? In my view, it makes no sense to do so, but the choice is yours," Posner wrote to Cartel.

Ultimately, Posner wrote to Cartel in April of this year: "Based on the tenor and content of your email, along with your previous communications with the members of my office, it is my respectful view there has been a breakdown in our solicitor-client relationship. Accordingly, I will be requesting to be removed from the record on the next court date."
Cartel replied: "I was going to terminate your services Monday, in any event…. I have long ago lost any faith that you or your firm could represent my best interests."

items: Toronto lawyer couple sentenced to jail for contempt over millions in missing homebuyer funds
Lawyer who admitted stealing millions of dollars from homeowners is disbarred

blocks.text: Cartel told CBC News on Monday, on the sidelines of his trial, that he and Posner had settled their dispute out of court.

He is representing himself in his criminal trial. The judge, Rachel Grinburg, referred to that fact in court several times Monday, emphasizing that she wanted to ensure the proceedings were fair to him.

His law licence has been provisionally suspended since April 2024 by the Law Society of Ontario, which has levelled 20 disciplinary accusations against him, including 12 counts of misappropriation of client funds.
Bui was disbarred by the Law Society in December.

articles.title: Measles cases are spreading in the US this year, with over 1,000 infections reported in Pennsylvania
articles.summary: A measles outbreak in Pennsylvania has topped 1,000 cases, with neighboring New York declaring a disaster emergency and mobilizing measures to fight the spread.

image.caption: A child receives a measles vaccine during an outbreak in Texas last year [FILE: Feb 27, 2025]Image: Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Over 1,000 cases of measles have been recorded so far this year in Pennsylvania alone, health officials in the northeastern US state said on Monday, the largest outbreak in a US state since the early 1990s.
The US Center for Disease Control (CDC) has put the number of cases recorded nationwide so far this year at 3,869, in what is seen as the worst year for measles since 1991.
What do we know about the latest measles outbreak?

The current outbreak started west of Philadelphia in April, health officials said. Nearly 200 people have been hospitalized and five have died. Nearly all of the cases involved people who were not vaccinated, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health.
In neighboring New York on Monday, Governor Kathy Hochul declared a month-long state disaster emergency to "strengthen ongoing efforts to confront" measles.
Over 100 cases have been recorded this year in New York State outside of New York City, with 92 of those reported in "under-immunized" rural areas since July 15.
The executive order suspends regulations on administering vaccines, expanding permission to paramedics and midwives, while allowing nurses to order testing and lowering permission barriers.
"No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease," Hochul said.
US vaccine coverage dips
Since last year, measles has broken out in several US states, including Texas, Utah and South Carolina, which has reported just under 1,000 cases.
Measles includes symptoms like high fever, cough, and rash. It can cause serious complications, especially in young children. It is highly contagious but can be prevented with vaccines.
However, skepticism toward vaccines in the US has risen in recent years, with more parents waiving routine vaccinations amid disinformation about vaccine safety.
Is the US experiencing a vaccine crisis?
In 2000, the US had eliminated the domestic spread of measles with high vaccination rates, but coverage has recently dipped below the 95% necessary to prevent outbreaks.

US Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr, who has expressed views skeptical of vaccines that are not backed by science, has characterized vaccinations as a "personal choice."

Although Kennedy maintains that the measles vaccine is the best defense against the highly contagious and potentially fatal infection, he has also advocated unproven "alternative treatments" like taking vitamins.

articles.title: Sergeant found not guilty of assaulting military police officers who removed her from 17 Wing
articles.summary: A Royal Canadian Air Force sergeant who refused to leave a restricted area of Winnipeg's 17 Wing has been found not guilty of assaulting the military police officers who had removed her from the base…

image.caption: Sgt. Athena Morris has been found not guilty of assaulting three members of the military police at 17 Wing in Winnipeg. The decision was handed down by military Judge Col. Stephen Strickey at HMCS Chippawa on Monday. (Santiago Arias Orozco/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba

A Royal Canadian Air Force sergeant who refused to leave a restricted area of Winnipeg's 17 Wing has been found not guilty of assaulting the military police officers who had removed her from the base using what a martial court ruled involved the use of excessive force.
Sgt. Athena Morris intended to bring attention to important issue but showed lack of judgment, judge ruled
However, Sgt. Athena Morris has been ordered to pay a fine for unlawfully entering the space to conduct a "peaceful protest" that required police intervention.

"Your intent was to bring attention to an important issue that affected you personally," military Judge Col. Stephen Strickey said Monday before a court martial held at HMCS Chippawa, a Royal Canadian Navy reserve division in Winnipeg.
"However, as a senior non-commissioned member of the CAF with 20 years of service … this was a regrettable lack of judgment on your part."

Court has heard that Morris jumped over a service counter and, using a scarf, tied herself to a chair in an administrative space that was off-limits to the public, known as the orderly room, after she was denied a request to change her gender marker on the Canadian Armed Forces' national human resources records system on March 31, 2025.
Three military police officers repeatedly asked her to leave, but Morris said she wouldn't do it until her information was updated, according to an agreed statement of circumstances read Monday.

The officers handcuffed Morris and placed her in the back of a cruiser where she was shocked with an energy conductive weapon. She was charged with assaulting a police officer and with resisting or escaping from arrest or custody.
Police conduct doesn't excuse sergeant's actions: prosecutor

Morris filed an application alleging her Charter rights were infringed during the arrest. The court found the military police had used excessive force and failed to provide reasonable assistance to facilitate her access to counsel while she was in hospital.
The court determined a sentence reduction was the "appropriate remedy" in light of the Charter breaches.

Maj. Laurent Carignan told court the prosecution accepted the ruling and on Monday they didn't present evidence on the three separate counts Morris initially faced for allegedly assaulting a police officer — so she was found not guilty.
The Charter violation was also an "essential component" to a joint recommendation by the prosecution and defence to sentence Morris to a $2,000 fine, Carignan said.

Morris pleaded guilty to entering a restricted administrative workspace on the base without authorization and refusing to leave until she was removed. Under the National Defence Act, the offence could carry a maximum punishment of dismissal from the Canadian Armed Forces with disgrace, according to the judge.
Carignan said Morris's misconduct does not excuse the "unconstitutional conduct" of the military police, but it also doesn't erase the seriousness of her actions.

"Her chosen conduct was serious," Carignan told court. "The prosecution recognizes the administrative issue was important and deeply personal to her. But its importance did not authorize her to enter a restricted workplace and remain there until she was forcibly removed."
'Ongoing pattern of discrimination': Morris

Morris told the court martial the events leading up to her arrest didn't occur in isolation, but against a broader backdrop of ongoing disputes concerning her gender identity transition within the Armed Forces.

The sergeant said she had been ordered to stop using the women's washroom and instead use the men's shower facility. Morris said the CAF declined to update her email address with her preferred name and when she went to the orderly room to have her gender marker corrected, it had already been at least four months of attempting to get it changed.
"I understood it in the context of what I had already experienced … an ongoing pattern of discrimination," she told court.
The issues continued following her arrest, Morris said. She was misgendered and called by her dead name in written communication, even after providing legal documentation with her new name, she said.

"What has caused much of the lasting harm has been the experience of identifying a problem, explaining why it was discriminatory or harmful, and then finding that the institutions or individuals involved were unwilling to reconsider their position," Morris said.
Defence counsel Maj. Carlos Da Cruz told court Morris's actions were not a random act of indiscipline, but an incident born of sheer exhaustion and desperation — without violence or threat of it.

"She was backed into a corner by a failure at the very institution tasked with assisting her," he said. "Her moral blameworthiness must be heavily mitigated by the fact that she was reacting to a persistent systemic failure to respect her human dignity."
Da Cruz said Morris has an otherwise clean record, filled with military accomplishments, and she did not consider the impact her actions had on the operations at the administrative space.

items: Sergeant tied herself to chair at Winnipeg's air force base after bid to change gender in records denied

blocks.text: But the prosecution argued Morris's behavior already had a "significant sustained negative impacts" on operations across multiple units — resorting to new protocols such as installing physical barriers and alarm systems in customer service areas.
"Military service demands self-discipline, emotional control, some judgment and professional conflict resolution. On this occasion, Sgt. Morris did not demonstrate those qualities," Naurent said.
Strickey said he agrees that a CAF member cannot respond in the way Morris did to an administrative area, regardless of the issue's importance.
The judge also said the focus on the sentence should be placed to deter other offenders from committing similar acts and acknowledged the harm done to the community.
"A fine of $2,000 would represent a meaningful sanction," Strickey's decision said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Santiago Arias Orozco is a journalist with CBC Manitoba currently based in Winnipeg. He previously worked for CBC Toronto and the Toronto Star. You can reach him at santiago.arias.orozco@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Did a Russian lab worker die from pneumonic plague? What we know — and don't know
articles.summary: An unnerving story has emerged from southeastern Russia involving the death of 28-year-old woman from pneumonia and fears that she may have been exposed to a form of plague at the lab where she…

image.caption: A view of the Medical Assistance and Rescue Centre, an infectious diseases hospital, in the town of Shelekhov in the Irkutsk region of Russia, on Oct. 5. (Stringer/Reuters)

blocks.text: Nearly 200 quarantined after researcher at Russian plague laboratory dies

An unnerving story has emerged from southeastern Russia involving the death of 28-year-old woman from pneumonia and fears that she may have been exposed to a form of plague at the lab where she worked.
Yes, plague — specifically, pneumonic plague.

Few details are confirmed. Russian authorities say there is currently no evidence that the illness was connected to any of the pathogens she worked with at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.
But the governor of a neighbouring region fuelled speculation over the weekend when he posted on Telegram suggesting the woman had died of plague, later altering his comment to include "maybe."

People have been quarantined at the hospital where she died last week; many others who came in contact with her were put under medical supervision, according to Anna Popova, Russia's public health agency.

There are, however, questions about Russian authorities' transparency, along with general shock at the thought of someone dying from an illness associated with the Middle Ages — and that many don't realize still exists.
Here's what we know and what we don't know about the situation in the Siberian city of Irkutsk, the lab worker who died and what Russian and other global officials are saying about the case.
What happened?
Russian state-run news agency TASS reported that the employee was "diagnosed with pneumonia of unknown etiology."
Local media reports have identified her as laboratory technician Darya Shipilova, saying she died on Friday.

The lab, which was established under the former Soviet Union in 1934, carries out scientific research on plague control, vaccine development and epidemic prevention, as well as work on other dangerous infectious diseases like cholera, brucellosis and anthrax.
CBC News has not independently confirmed Shipilova's identity or details about her work.

items: At 'crucial' moment for pandemic preparedness, experts say world isn't ready

blocks.text: Russian-language reports say that Shipilova went to a hospital in Shelekhov, about 20 kilometres southwest of Irkutsk, days before her death.

Per Ria Novosti, another state-run outlet, Irkutsk Region Governor Igor Kobzev announced on Friday that a resident had been diagnosed with a "a particularly dangerous infection" of an undetermined nature.
"Importantly, over the past few days, no new cases of staff from the Anti-Plague Institute seeking medical attention have been identified," Kobzev said.
What is pneumonic plague?

Plague, which came to be known as the Black Death when it ravaged Europe in the 1300s, is an infectious disease caused by a bacterium known as Yersinia pestis, or Y. pestis. It is carried by small mammals and generally spread by the fleas that feed off them.
Those fleas can transmit Y. pestis to humans and other large mammals.
There are three forms of plague: bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.

Bubonic plague, the most common form, causes buboes — painful, inflammed lymph nodes near the site of a flea bite. Symptoms usually come on after three to seven days, and can include fever, chills, headache and extreme exhaustion.

Septicemic plague happens when bubonic plague infections aren't treated and spread to the bloodstream and other parts of the body. It can cause vomiting, diarrhea, multiple organ failures and septic shock.
Pneumonic plague is when Y. pestis infects the lungs, making it much more of a risk because it can then be transmitted between people through airborne droplets.
Symptoms — including high fever, cough, coughing up blood and difficulty breathing — can occur within one to three days of inhalation. It can be fatal if left untreated.
How deadly is it?
Plague is easily treated with antibiotics, which did not exist during the Black Death, Dr. Malick Gibani, a clinical associate professor at Imperial College London, told CBC News.
But people do still die from it, he says, though that's generally restricted to certain geographic areas, often due to conditions that attract rodents, or the fact that they are remote.

Between 2019 and 2025, the World Health Organization (WHO) recorded 3,847 suspected cases and 423 deaths in 10 countries. Most of those infections occurred in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Madagascar.
In 2017, a pneumonic plague outbreak in the latter country affected more than 2,400 people and killed 209 people.
But Gibani notes that plague infections can occur in other parts of the world like parts of Russia, as well as in South America and and parts of the western U.S.
Siberia was the location of the first known prehistoric human outbreak of plague.
Do I need to be worried?

While there are still many unanswered questions, this possible outbreak is nothing like the COVID-19 pandemic because plague is "a much different pathogen," said Angela Rasmussen, a virologist at the University of Saskatchewan.
Even before they become sick, infected people are "constantly shedding" the virus that causes COVID-19, she said, which is how it spread so far.
"You're not going to be walking around feeling fine, shedding Yersinia pestis everywhere for everybody else to breathe in," she said.

items: Inside the Montreal lab preparing Canada for the next pandemic

blocks.text: In fact, you should be more concerned about coming into contact with an infected rodent than getting an infection potentially from a lab in Siberia, she says.
Even though it's not been officially confirmed that Shipilova died of pneumonic plague, Gibani says a rapid response is key to controlling the spread in any situation like this.
He says that can include contact tracing and offering antibiotics to those who may have been identified as being at risk of exposure.
LISTEN | Where scientists believe they found ground zero for 'Black Death':
Quirks and Quarks8:08The Black Death was history’s most lethal plague. Now we know where it started
How is the rest of the world reacting?
Russian officials have sought to quell fears about a possible outbreak.

But some countries, such as Kazakhstan, aren't taking chances and are raising alerts or implementing quarantine at border crossings. Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan have implemented similar measures even though they don't share borders with Russia.
The WHO is in contact Russian health authorities and has offered support if needed, a spokesperson said in a statement to CBC News.

items: Earliest outbreak of the plague killed hunter-gatherer kids 5,500 years ago

blocks.text: U.S. President Donald Trump also said his administration would also offer assistance.

"Anybody that has that kind of a problem, we're always willing to help," Trump told reporters as he left the White House for a trip to Nebraska, calling the possible outbreak a "big problem for Russia."
Health Canada told CBC it is also monitoring the situation, though it sees no risk to Canada at this time. According to the agency, the last recorded human case of plague in this country was in 1939.
